a-2026-09-16-0001.body_html: The rank formula is stated for the underlying graph's component count, but nothing in the statement says that a loop counts as an arrow and contributes to the rank. Arden is explicit about it on page 2; say so here too.

a-2026-09-16-0002.body_html: The kernel--image count is right but compressed into one clause. A reader checking it has to supply the rank--nullity step and the saturation step themselves. A replacement is attached.
a-2026-09-16-0002.payload: the sequence $0 \to \Zcyc(\quiv) \to W(\quiv) \to \operatorname{im} \bd \to 0$ is exact and $\operatorname{im} \bd$ is free, so it splits and the ranks add
a-2026-09-16-0002.quote: the rank of the kernel is the rank of the source less the rank of the image

a-2026-09-16-0003.body_html: Integrality of the vertices of \(\Pi\) does not follow from saturation of the cycle lattice: saturation is about the lattice, integrality is about the polytope's vertices, and Bellamy assumes the second (the balancing hypothesis). This is the gap Lemma~sh-000E is meant to close, and it is not closed.
a-2026-09-16-0003.quote: since $\Pi$ has integral vertices by the saturation of Proposition~\ref{sh-0007}

a-2026-09-16-0004.body_html: Is the walk required to be a walk in the quiver, or only in the support? The two differ when an arrow of weight zero joins two arrows of the support.
a-2026-09-16-0004.quote: we obtain an infinite walk inside $\supp(w)$

a-2026-09-16-0005.body_html: Worth naming the quotient here: it is the group the divergence map lands in, and it is used twice later.
a-2026-09-16-0005.payload: The quotient $W(\quiv)/\Zcyc(\quiv)$ is the \emph{boundary lattice} of $\quiv$.

a-2026-09-16-0006.body_html: The paper never says whether quivers are assumed connected. Convention~sh-0001 says finite and says nothing about connectedness, and the rank formula is the only place it would matter.

a-2026-09-16-0007.body_html: This section introduces the divergence map twice, once in prose and once as Definition sh-0003. Keep the definition.

a-2026-09-16-0008.body_html: The formula is right, and it is the one place the component count \(c\) appears without being defined in the same breath.

a-2026-09-16-0009.body_html: The transcription drops Arden's hypothesis that the quiver is finite, which is in his standing assumptions and not in the proposition. It is harmless here and would not be in a quilt that cited him for an infinite quiver.
a-2026-09-16-0009.quote: whose underlying graph has $c$ connected components

a-2026-09-16-0010.body_html: Both examples check out, and the second is the smallest quiver with trivial cycle lattice.

a-2026-09-16-0011.body_html: The infinite case has a standard reference; cite it rather than pointing at a survey.
a-2026-09-16-0011.payload: Cortez, Flows on infinite quivers: a survey, Bull. Imag. Soc. 2007, Section 5

a-2026-09-16-0012.body_html: The remark asserts that no index creeps in, which is what Proposition sh-0007 says; the remark is redundant.
a-2026-09-16-0012.discard_reason: Proposition sh-0007 is a proposition and the remark is a remark; they are allowed to say the same thing.

a-2026-09-16-0013.body_html: Height is defined for every weighting but only used for balanced ones, and \(N_{\quiv}(k)\) silently restricts to them. Say so in the definition rather than in the theorem that uses it.

a-2026-09-16-0014.body_html: This proof uses that the target of the divergence map is torsion-free, which is true of \(\ZZ^{V}\) and is never said. One clause fixes it.
a-2026-09-16-0014.quote: a homomorphism into a torsion-free group

a-2026-09-16-0015.body_html: A loop contributes an arrow and no divergence, so it adds one to the rank. I will say it in Convention sh-0001 rather than in the theorem.

a-2026-09-16-0016.body_html: Then the convention is the right place, and this finding can stand until it is there.

a-2026-09-16-0017.body_html: Does this need the quiver to be connected, or does the component count handle it?
a-2026-09-16-0017.quote: A quiver whose underlying graph is a forest

a-2026-09-16-0018.body_html: Read against the definition in Arden24-def-1.2; the two agree.

a-2026-09-17-0001.body_html: I would split this: the polynomiality and the degree are two claims and only the first needs Bellamy.

a-2026-09-17-0002.body_html: Agreed that this is the gap. I will not accept sh-000C until sh-000E is proved.
a-2026-09-17-0002.quote: since $\Pi$ has integral vertices by the saturation of Proposition~\ref{sh-0007}

a-2026-09-17-0003.body_html: A quiver should be required to be connected.

a-2026-09-17-0005.body_html: This is the form we use; the balanced case is the one that matters here.

a-2026-09-17-0006.body_html: Does this need the weights to be integral, or only bounded?

a-2026-09-17-0007.body_html: Is total unimodularity really needed here, or only that the vertices are integral?

a-2026-09-17-0008.body_html: This is the display we cite; the balanced case is the one that matters.
a-2026-09-17-0008.quote: Proposition 3.1. The function L is a quasi-polynomial in k of degree equal to the dimension of M (D), with a period dividing the least common multiple of the denominators of the vertices of M (D).

a-2026-09-17-0009.body_html: Answered on the page: unimodularity is the mechanism, integrality of the vertices is what is used downstream.
a-2026-09-17-0009.quote: the constraint matrix is an incidence matrix

a-2026-09-17-0010.body_html: Please verify the transcription of 3.2 against p.2: the digest says 'integral' where the page says 'bounded'.

Bellamy19-def-4.1.source_text: The defect of a weighted digraph is the least common multiple of the denominators of the vertices of its median polytope.

Bellamy19-prop-3.1.page_text:
We now count. The dilate kM (D) of the median polytope is the set of points kx with x in
M (D), and L(k) denotes the number of points of ZA in it.
Proposition 3.1. The function L is a quasi-polynomial in k of degree equal to the dimension
of M (D), with a period dividing the least common multiple of the denominators of the vertices
of M (D).
Proof. This is Ehrhart’s theorem for a rational polytope, applied to M (D), together with the
observation that the dimension of the dilate is the dimension of the polytope.
Theorem 3.2. Let D be a weighted digraph whose weight function is balanced at every vertex.
Then the counting function of the median polytope of D agrees with a polynomial of degree
equal to the dimension of that polytope for every nonnegative integer dilation factor, and the
leading coefficient of that polynomial is the relative volume of the polytope.
Proof. By Theorem 2.3 the polytope is the convex hull of integral vertices, so its Ehrhart
quasi-polynomial has period one, and Proposition 3.1 then gives a polynomial of the stated
degree. The statement about the leading coefficient is the standard interpretation of the
Bellamy19-prop-3.1.source_text: The function L is a quasi-polynomial in k of degree equal to the dimension of M (D), with a period dividing the least common multiple of the denominators of the vertices of M (D).
Bellamy19-prop-3.1.statement: The function $L$ is a quasi-polynomial in $k$ of degree equal to the dimension of $M(D)$, with a period dividing the least common multiple of the denominators of the vertices of $M(D)$.

Bellamy19-thm-2.3.source_text: The median orders of a weighted digraph are in bijection with the vertices of a rational polytope M (D) ⊆ RA cut out by the exchange inequalities of Lemma 2.2, and M (D) is bounded.
